question:
Patient note:
A 62-year-old man with longstanding type 2 diabetes mellitus complicated by peripheral neuropathy, non-valvular atrial fibrillation treated with apixaban, ischemic cardiomyopathy with a remote left anterior descending stent, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease was transported to the emergency department by county advanced life-support ambulance after his spouse heard a heavy thud in the upstairs bathroom at 06:40 and found him supine on the tile floor, eyes shut, snoring softly, and surrounded by scattered toiletries but no overt blood or vomitus. She reports he had risen at 05:50 complaining only of “a light head.” First responders reached the home seven minutes after the 911 call, applied a rigid cervical collar, positioned him on a scoop stretcher, and inserted a single 18-gauge IV in the left antecubital vein that was flushed with 5 mL saline only; they delivered 10 L/min oxygen by non-rebreather, recorded a fingertip glucose of 108 mg/dL, and intentionally withheld dextrose, naloxone, benzodiazepines, opioids, neuromuscular blockers, sedatives, antihypertensives, vasopressors, or hyperosmolar agents so that an undisturbed neurologic examination could be obtained on hospital arrival. Continuous cardiac monitoring en route showed atrial fibrillation with ventricular response 86–92 beats/min, and no arrhythmia therapy was attempted during the eleven-minute transport. On roll-in to our resuscitation bay at 07:08, prior to any in-house intervention, vital signs measured concurrently with the first neurologic survey are blood pressure 144/82 mm Hg by automated cuff on the right arm, heart rate 90 beats/min in irregularly irregular rhythm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min with shallow abdominal excursion, oxygen saturation 97 % on the pre-hospital mask, and rectal temperature 36.4 °C. Airway inspection reveals an intact dentition, midline uvula, moist mucosa, and brisk gag when a tongue depressor grazes the posterior pharyngeal wall; breath sounds are vesicular and equal bilaterally without stridor or wheeze, though there is faint snoring audible when the mandible is allowed to fall posteriorly. Pupils are 3 mm, round, equally centered, and constrict promptly to direct and consensual light. During a silent thirty-second observation his eyelids remain shut without flutter; when the trauma nurse states his first name in a normal conversational tone at the bedside the lids separate to about two-thirds full aperture, irides drift briefly toward the speaker, and after several seconds they drift closed again. Repetition of his name at louder volume recreates the same limited opening; without voice stimulus the lids stay closed. Speech is sparse yet intelligible: when asked “What is your name?” he responds, “I live… where is the bus?,” and to “Do you know where you are?” he mutters, “Need to go work, can’t be late,” failing to supply correct orientation to place, date, or circumstance, and answers are tangential and disorganized. Cranial nerve testing is otherwise notable for symmetrical facial grimace to deep mandibular angle pinch and a cough provoked by tracheal palpation; corneal reflexes are intact. Upper and lower extremities lie flaccid in slight external rotation. A firm supra-orbital notch pressure for ten seconds produces no visible movement of shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, or ankles; nail-bed compression on all four extremities, bilateral trapezius squeeze, and sternal rub similarly fail to elicit even a twitch or withdrawal. Palpable muscle tone is low throughout, joints move freely without spasticity or rigidity, and no involuntary posturing, tremor, or myoclonic jerk is observed. Deep tendon reflexes at biceps, triceps, patellae, and Achilles are absent, plantar stimulation yields no toe movement, and there is no ankle clonus. Cardiovascular examination shows variable S1 intensity consistent with his chronic arrhythmia but no murmurs, rubs, or gallops; distal pulses are 2 + bilaterally with capillary refill under two seconds and warm, well-perfused skin. Abdomen is flat, soft, and nontender with active bowel sounds; pelvis is stable on gentle compression, and rectal tone is scant though present. Secondary survey reveals a 4 cm hematoma over the occipital scalp without laceration, several ecchymoses across the lumbar region likely from the fall, and no long-bone deformities; there is no Battle sign, orbital ecchymosis, or otorrhea. A bedside eFAST performed within five minutes shows no intraperitoneal, pericardial, or pleural free fluid. Point-of-care arterial blood gas on the current oxygen mask demonstrates pH 7.36, PaCO₂ 37 mm Hg, PaO₂ 104 mm Hg, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, and base excess −2 mEq/L. Serum electrolytes, complete blood count, coagulation profile (including anti-Xa level), troponin, ethanol, and urine toxicology have been drawn but are pending. No intravenous fluids, analgesics, sedative-hypnotics, paralytics, anticonvulsants, antihypertensives, vasopressors, hyperosmolar medications, or reversal agents have yet been administered, ensuring that the neurologic findings—eyelid opening only when addressed by voice, disoriented speech, and complete absence of limb or trunk movement despite robust painful stimuli—represent his untreated baseline at presentation. Neurosurgery, neurology, and critical care have been paged emergently; non-contrast head CT, CT angiography of neck vessels, and cervical spine CT are ordered stat, and airway equipment is positioned at bedside should declining protective reflexes necessitate rapid-sequence intubation while serial neurologic checks occur every fifteen minutes.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow Coma Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow Coma Scale sums the best eye (1–4), verbal (1–5), and motor (1–6) responses on the untreated admission exam.
- Eye: His eyes remain closed until his name is spoken. Opening to voice scores E3.
- Verbal: He answers questions with intelligible phrases but is disoriented. Confused conversation scores V4.
- Motor: There is no limb movement to any pressure stimulus. The facial grimace does not count as limb withdrawal. This scores M1.
Total = 3 + 4 + 1 = 8.
Final answer: 8
